subject: community-medicine
title: Influenza: Antigenic Change, Pandemics and Prevention

steps.title: A segmented virus wearing two spikes
steps.tx: The **influenza virus** is an orthomyxovirus with eight segments of single stranded RNA and two surface glycoproteins, haemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N), which name each subtype such as H1N1 or H3N2. Types A and B cause seasonal epidemics, type A alone causes pandemics, and type C causes only mild sporadic illness that programmes ignore.
steps.say: Eight RNA segments, two spikes. Haemagglutinin and neuraminidase name the subtype, type A alone makes pandemics, and type C is clinically trivial.

steps.title: Drift: the yearly small change
steps.tx: **Antigenic drift** is the gradual accumulation of point mutations in the haemagglutinin and neuraminidase genes during ordinary replication. Antibody from last season partly fails, so the same subtype returns each winter in slightly altered form. Drift explains annual epidemics and why vaccine strains are reviewed and updated every year for both hemispheres.
steps.say: Drift is slow point mutation. Last year's antibody partly fails, epidemics return yearly, and vaccine strains need annual review. Small change, yearly consequence.

rows: Point mutations in H and N genes

steps.title: Shift: the pandemic change
steps.tx: **Antigenic shift** is an abrupt reassortment of gene segments when two different influenza A viruses infect one cell, often in pigs mixing avian and human strains. A wholly new haemagglutinin appears against which the population has almost no immunity. Shift produced the 1918 H1N1, 1957 H2N2, 1968 H3N2 and 2009 pandemic waves.
steps.say: Shift swaps whole segments in a co-infected host. A new haemagglutinin meets a non-immune population, and a pandemic follows. Remember the four pandemic years.

steps.tx: **Antigenic shift** is an abrupt reassortment of gene segments when two different influenza A viruses infect one cell, often a pig mixing avian and human strains. A wholly new haemagglutinin appears, and the population has almost no immunity against it. That mechanism produced the 1918 H1N1 pandemic, the 1957 H2N2 pandemic, the 1968 H3N2 pandemic, and the 2009 pandemic wave marked on the timeline.
steps.say: When two influenza A viruses infect one cell, often in a pig, whole gene segments reassort and a new haemagglutinin appears. Almost no one is immune. That shift sits behind 1918 H1N1, 1957 H2N2, 1968 H3N2, and 2009.

steps.title: Incubation, infectivity and the clinical picture
steps.tx: The **incubation period** of influenza is short, usually 18 to 72 hours, and patients shed virus from a day before symptoms until about five days after onset. Abrupt fever, headache, myalgia and dry cough dominate, quite unlike the gradual coryza of a common cold. Most cases settle in a week without antibiotics.
steps.say: One to three days of incubation, shedding starts before symptoms. Abrupt fever with myalgia separates flu from a cold, and most cases need no antibiotic.

rows: Day before to 5 days after onset

steps.title: Who dies of flu: the risk groups
steps.tx: **Complications** concentrate in the extremes of age, pregnancy, obesity and chronic heart, lung, kidney or metabolic disease, plus immunosuppression. Primary viral pneumonia and secondary staphylococcal or pneumococcal pneumonia cause most deaths, with myocarditis and encephalitis much rarer. These same groups head every vaccination priority list in national guidance.
steps.say: Deaths cluster in the old, the pregnant, the obese and the chronically ill. Pneumonia, viral or secondary bacterial, kills most often, so those groups vaccinate first.

steps.title: Swine flu and avian flu in one line each
steps.tx: **H1N1 influenza** from the 2009 pandemic is now a seasonal strain covered by routine vaccines and treated supportively, with oseltamivir reserved early for severe or high risk cases. Avian H5N1 and H7N9 spill over from poultry with high case fatality but poor human to human spread, so exposure history drives suspicion.
steps.say: Pandemic H1N1 became seasonal. Avian strains spill from poultry, kill often, but spread poorly between people. Ask about bird exposure whenever the picture fits.

steps.title: Vaccines: killed, live and who gets them
steps.tx: The **inactivated influenza vaccine** is grown in eggs or cell culture, given intramuscularly each year, and safe in pregnancy and immunosuppression. Live attenuated vaccine is sprayed intranasally for healthy children and young adults in some countries. Health workers, risk groups and pregnant women are the standing priority categories for annual doses.
steps.say: Killed vaccine yearly by injection is safe in pregnancy. Live spray suits healthy children where used. Health workers and risk groups stand first in the queue.

steps.title: Chemoprophylaxis and outbreak control
steps.tx: **Oseltamivir prophylaxis** uses a neuraminidase inhibitor once daily for at least seven days after exposure, offered to high risk contacts and during closed setting outbreaks in care homes. It complements, never replaces, vaccination and isolation of cases for five days. Hand hygiene and cough etiquette cut droplet spread in wards and schools.
steps.say: Post-exposure oseltamivir runs at least a week for high risk contacts. Isolate cases five days, push hygiene, and still vaccinate. Prophylaxis complements the vaccine.

steps.title: Surveillance: how the world watches flu
steps.tx: **Influenza surveillance** networks track influenza like illness and severe acute respiratory infection through sentinel sites, confirm strains in laboratories, and feed the twice yearly vaccine strain selection. Sudden rises in severe respiratory admissions, clusters in schools, or deaths in health workers are the signals that trigger outbreak investigation and public messaging.
steps.say: Sentinel surveillance plus laboratory confirmation picks next season's vaccine strains. Watch severe admissions and clusters closely; they announce the wave before routine counts do.
